vtrmc-2013-01.title: Half-angle substitution
vtrmc-2013-01.body:
For $0\le t<\pi$, $\sqrt{1+\cos t}=\sqrt{2\cos^2\frac t2}=\sqrt2\cos\frac t2$ and $17-8\cos t=17-8\left(1-2\sin^2\frac t2\right)=9+16\sin^2\frac t2$. So
$$I=\int_0^x\frac{6\cos\frac t2}{9+16\sin^2\frac t2}\,dt .$$
Put $z=\sin\frac t2$, $dz=\frac12\cos\frac t2\,dt$:
$$I=\int_0^{\sin(x/2)}\frac{12\,dz}{9+16z^2}=\Big[\arctan\frac{4z}{3}\Big]_0^{\sin(x/2)}=\arctan\left(\frac43\sin\frac x2\right).$$
For $0<x<\pi$ this lies in $(0,\frac\pi2)$, so $\tan I=\frac43\sin\frac x2$. The condition $\frac43\sin\frac x2=\frac2{\sqrt3}$ gives $\sin\frac x2=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, and since $0<\frac x2<\frac\pi2$, $\frac x2=\frac\pi3$.

**Answer: $x=\frac{2\pi}3$.**

vtrmc-2013-02.title: Difference of two angles
vtrmc-2013-02.body:
Scale so that $BC=1$ and put $DB=x>0$, $AD=2x$, $AB=3x$. Since $\angle ABC=90^\circ$,
$$\angle BCA=\arctan(3x),\qquad\angle BCD=\arctan x,$$
and $D$ lies between $A$ and $B$, so $\theta=\angle ACD=\arctan3x-\arctan x\in(0^\circ,90^\circ)$. By the subtraction formula,
$$\tan\theta=\frac{3x-x}{1+3x^2}=\frac{2x}{1+3x^2}\le\frac{2x}{2\sqrt3\,x}=\frac1{\sqrt3},$$
by AM-GM ($1+3x^2\ge2\sqrt3x$), with equality iff $3x^2=1$. Since $\tan$ is increasing on $(0^\circ,90^\circ)$, $\theta\le30^\circ$, with equality when $AB=\sqrt3\,BC$.

**Answer: $30^\circ$.**

vtrmc-2013-02.title: Area of triangle $ADC$ (official approach)
vtrmc-2013-02.body:
With $BC=1$, $BD=x$, $AD=2x$, let $\theta=\angle ACD$, $y=AC$, $z=DC$. The area of $\triangle ADC$ is $\frac12\cdot AD\cdot BC=x$ and also $\frac12yz\sin\theta$. With $y^2=1+9x^2$ and $z^2=1+x^2$,
$$\sin^2\theta=\frac{4x^2}{(1+9x^2)(1+x^2)}=\frac{4}{x^{-2}+10+9x^2}.$$
Maximising $\theta$ (acute) means minimising $x^{-2}+9x^2\ge2\sqrt9=6$, with equality at $x^2=\frac13$. Then $\sin^2\theta=\frac4{16}=\frac14$, so the maximum is $\theta=30^\circ$.

**Answer: $30^\circ$.**

vtrmc-2013-03.title: Take logarithms twice
vtrmc-2013-03.body:
**Yes.** By induction $a_n>1$, so $\ln a_n>0$, and
$$\ln a_{n+1}=\left(1+n^{-3/2}\right)\ln a_n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\ln a_n=\ln2\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1+k^{-3/2}\right).$$
Taking logarithms again and using $\ln(1+t)\le t$,
$$\ln\ln a_n=\ln\ln2+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\ln\left(1+k^{-3/2}\right)\le\ln\ln2+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-3/2}<\infty,$$
since $\sum k^{-3/2}$ converges ($p$-series with $p=\frac32>1$). So $(a_n)$ is bounded. It is also increasing, because $a_n>1$ and the exponent $1+n^{-3/2}>1$ give $a_{n+1}>a_n$. A bounded increasing sequence converges.

(The limit is finite; numerically $a_n\approx572$ for large $n$.)

**Answer: Yes, $(a_n)$ converges.**

vtrmc-2013-04.title: Primes $3\bmod 4$ and infinite descent
vtrmc-2013-04.body:
**(a)** $25=\dfrac{50}{2}=\dfrac{5^2+5^2}{1^2+1^2}$.

**Lemma.** If $p\equiv3\pmod4$ is prime and $p\mid x^2+y^2$, then $p\mid x$ and $p\mid y$.

*Proof.* If $p\nmid x$, then $x^2\equiv-y^2$ forces $p\nmid y$ too. Write $p-1=2(2k+1)$. Raising $x^2\equiv-y^2$ to the odd power $\frac{p-1}2=2k+1$ gives $x^{p-1}\equiv-y^{p-1}\pmod p$. By Fermat both sides are $\equiv1$ and $\equiv-1$, so $p\mid2$, impossible. $\square$

**(b)** $2013=3\cdot11\cdot61$. Suppose $x^2+y^2=2013(u^2+v^2)$ with positive integers, and choose such a solution with $x^2+y^2$ minimal. Since $3\mid x^2+y^2$, the lemma gives $x=3x_1$, $y=3y_1$. Then
$$9(x_1^2+y_1^2)=3\cdot671\,(u^2+v^2)\ \Longrightarrow\ 3(x_1^2+y_1^2)=671(u^2+v^2).$$
As $3\nmid671=11\cdot61$, we get $3\mid u^2+v^2$, so $u=3u_1$, $v=3v_1$ by the lemma, and $x_1^2+y_1^2=2013(u_1^2+v_1^2)$. This is a solution in positive integers with $x_1^2+y_1^2=\frac{x^2+y^2}9<x^2+y^2$, contradicting minimality. So $2013$ is not special.

**(c)** $2014=2\cdot19\cdot53$ and $19\equiv3\pmod4$. The same argument with $p=19$ works: from $x^2+y^2=2014(u^2+v^2)$ we get $19\mid x,y$, then $19(x_1^2+y_1^2)=106(u^2+v^2)$ with $19\nmid106$, so $19\mid u,v$, and we obtain a smaller solution. So $2014$ is not special. ∎

vtrmc-2013-04.title: Counting the exponent of $p$
vtrmc-2013-04.body:
Part (a) is as before. Iterating the lemma of the first solution: if $p\equiv3\pmod4$ and $p^{e}\,\|\,x^2+y^2$ with $(x,y)\neq(0,0)$, then $e$ is **even** (divide $x,y$ by $p$ as long as $p$ divides $x^2+y^2$; each step removes $p^2$, and the process stops at a sum not divisible by $p$).

If $n(u^2+v^2)=x^2+y^2$ and $p\equiv3\pmod4$, then the exponent of $p$ in $n$ equals (even) $-$ (even), so it is even. But $3$ appears in $2013=3\cdot11\cdot61$ to the first power, and $19$ appears in $2014=2\cdot19\cdot53$ to the first power. Hence neither $2013$ nor $2014$ is special. (In fact, $n$ is special exactly when $n$ is a sum of two squares.) ∎

vtrmc-2013-05.title: Tangent substitution and Jensen
vtrmc-2013-05.body:
Write $x=\tan A$, $y=\tan B$, $z=\tan C$ with $A,B,C\in(0,\frac\pi2)$. Then $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\dfrac{\tan A}{\sec A}=\sin A$, etc.

**$A+B+C=\pi$.** If $xy=1$ then $x+y+z=xyz=z$, impossible as $x+y>0$. So $z(xy-1)=x+y>0$, hence $xy>1$ and
$$\tan C=z=-\frac{x+y}{1-xy}=-\tan(A+B)=\tan(\pi-A-B).$$
Because $\tan A\tan B>1$ means $\tan A>\cot B=\tan(\frac\pi2-B)$, we have $A+B>\frac\pi2$, so $\pi-A-B\in(0,\frac\pi2)$. As $\tan$ is injective on $(0,\frac\pi2)$, $C=\pi-A-B$.

**Jensen.** $\sin$ is concave on $[0,\pi]$, so
$$\frac{\sin A+\sin B+\sin C}{3}\le\sin\frac{A+B+C}{3}=\sin\frac\pi3=\frac{\sqrt3}2 .$$
Hence the left side is at most $\frac{3\sqrt3}2$, with equality iff $A=B=C=\frac\pi3$, i.e. $x=y=z=\sqrt3$. ∎

vtrmc-2013-05.title: Tangent-line bound instead of Jensen
vtrmc-2013-05.body:
After the substitution above it suffices to show $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C\le\frac{3\sqrt3}2$ for $A,B,C\in(0,\frac\pi2)$ with $A+B+C=\pi$. Since $\sin$ is concave on $[0,\pi]$, its graph lies below its tangent line at $\frac\pi3$:
$$\sin t\le\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac12\left(t-\frac\pi3\right)\qquad(0\le t\le\pi).$$
Adding this for $t=A,B,C$, the linear terms add up to $\frac12(A+B+C-\pi)=0$, so $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C\le\frac{3\sqrt3}2$. ∎

vtrmc-2013-06.title: Hua's identity $B=X-XYX$
vtrmc-2013-06.body:
**Claim.** $B=X-XYX$.

Since $Y^{-1}-X=Y^{-1}(I-YX)$ and $A$ is invertible, $I-YX$ is invertible and $A^{-1}=(I-YX)^{-1}Y$. Then
$$(X^{-1}+A^{-1})(X-XYX)=I-YX+(I-YX)^{-1}YX(I-YX).$$
Because $YX$ commutes with $I-YX$, we have $YX(I-YX)=(I-YX)YX$, so the last term is $YX$, and the product is $I$. Hence $X-XYX$ is the inverse of $X^{-1}+A^{-1}$, i.e. $B=X-XYX$.

**Conclusion.**
$$XY-BY=(X-B)Y=XYXY=(XY)^2,$$
so $M=XY$ works. Computing,
$$M=XY=\begin{pmatrix}7&8&9\\8&-9&-7\\-7&-7&9\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}9&8&-9\\8&-7&7\\7&9&8\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}190&81&65\\-49&64&-191\\-56&74&86\end{pmatrix}.$$
(For example, the $(1,1)$ entry is $63+64+63=190$.) A direct computer check with these $X,Y$ confirms $(XY)^2=XY-BY$. $M=-XY$ also works.

vtrmc-2013-07.title: Expand as a double series and swap indices
vtrmc-2013-07.body:
Let $r=\frac14$. Since $(2^n\pm2^{-n})^2=4^n(1\pm r^n)^2$,
$$\frac{n}{(2^n+2^{-n})^2}=\frac{n\,r^n}{(1+r^n)^2},\qquad\frac{n}{(2^n-2^{-n})^2}=\frac{n\,r^n}{(1-r^n)^2}.$$
For $|t|<1$, differentiating the geometric series gives $\frac{t}{(1-t)^2}=\sum_{k\ge1}kt^k$ and $\frac{t}{(1+t)^2}=\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k+1}kt^k$. Hence the sum is
$$S=\sum_{n\ge1}\sum_{k\ge1}nk\,r^{nk}\Big((-1)^{k+1}+(-1)^n\Big).$$
This double series converges absolutely: $nk\ge n+k-1\ge\frac{n+k}2$ (as $(n-1)(k-1)\ge0$), so $nk\,r^{nk}\le nk\,r^{(n+k)/2}=nk\,2^{-n-k}$, and $\sum_{n,k}nk\,2^{-n-k}=\left(\sum_n n\,2^{-n}\right)^2=4$. So we may rearrange freely. Renaming $(n,k)\to(k,n)$ in the first part,
$$\sum_{n,k}nk\,r^{nk}(-1)^{k+1}=\sum_{n,k}nk\,r^{nk}(-1)^{n+1},$$
and therefore
$$S=\sum_{n,k}nk\,r^{nk}\Big((-1)^{n+1}+(-1)^n\Big)=0 .$$

**Answer: $0$.**

vtrmc-2013-07.title: Differentiate a Lambert-series identity (official approach)
vtrmc-2013-07.body:
Let $q>1$ and $r=1/q$. Expanding in geometric series (absolutely convergent double sums),
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{q^n+1}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{r^n}{1+r^n}=\sum_{n,k\ge1}(-1)^{k+1}r^{nk},\qquad -\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^n}{q^n-1}=\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{r^n}{1-r^n}=\sum_{n,k\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}r^{nk}.$$
Swapping $n\leftrightarrow k$ shows the two are equal:
$$-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^n}{q^n-1}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{q^n+1}\qquad(q>1).$$
Both series of derivatives converge uniformly on $[q_0,\infty)$ for any $q_0>1$, so we may differentiate termwise. Using
$$\frac{d}{dq}\frac1{q^n\mp1}=\frac{-nq^{n-1}}{(q^n\mp1)^2}=\frac{-n}{q\,(q^{n/2}\mp q^{-n/2})^2},$$
we get
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^nn}{q(q^{n/2}-q^{-n/2})^2}=-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n}{q(q^{n/2}+q^{-n/2})^2}.$$
With $q=4$, $q^{n/2}=2^n$, so the requested sum is $0$. (Numerically the partial sums tend to $0$ to many digits.)

**Answer: $0$.**
